title: The Floor Between Four and Five
deck: An elevator technician finds a landing that is missing from the building plans. Someone has been waiting there for the repair she promised to finish.

sections.title: The complaint
paragraphs: The complaint said the elevator stopped between four and five whenever it rained. Everyone else in the maintenance office had crossed it off as a sensor fault. Leah kept the work order because of the second sentence: A woman on the landing says she knows the technician.

She reached Calder House at six, carrying a tool bag and the sandwich she had forgotten to eat. The caretaker showed her five buttons, five floors, and a recent inspection certificate. 'People hear the brakes,' he said. 'They make up the rest.' Then he asked whether she would be finished before dark.

On the fourth floor Leah found a fresh scrape inside the door track. She measured the leveling sensor, cleaned its bracket, and ran the car twice. Nothing unusual happened. Outside the stairwell window, rain began tapping the glass. The car made a third trip without her pressing a button.

It stopped where the floor indicator should have changed from four to five. Instead, the display went blank. The doors opened on a narrow landing with brown wallpaper and a pair of muddy children's boots drying on newspaper. At the far end, a woman in a green cardigan sat beside a radiator.

Leah recognized the cardigan before she recognized her mother. Her mother had been wearing it the afternoon Leah left for her apprenticeship, eleven years before she died. 'You've brought your tools,' the woman said. 'I thought you would.'

sections.title: The loose handle
paragraphs: Leah wedged the doors with her bag. It was a bad habit she corrected in younger technicians, but her hands had begun working without instruction. She stepped onto the landing. Behind her, the motor hummed with a steady electrical note. Ahead, a saucepan rattled on a stove she could not see.

Her mother pointed at a door with a loose brass handle. 'You said you'd fix that before you went.' Leah had. She remembered the stripped screw turning uselessly in her fingers, her mother insisting that the taxi was waiting, the irritating relief of being allowed to leave something unfinished.

She took out a screwdriver. The screw head was soft with age, its slot almost gone. While she worked, her mother asked about her flat, her difficult shoulder, the job Leah had considered leaving. She knew ordinary things that had happened after her death. Leah kept looking up to find the trick in her face.

There was no trick. The woman had the small burn on her wrist from a baking tray, the crooked tooth she hid in photographs. When she smiled, Leah wanted to put down the screwdriver and lean her forehead against that familiar cardigan. Instead she asked where this landing went.

'Home,' her mother said. She nodded at the door. Warm light showed beneath it. Leah heard a chair scrape the kitchen floor, followed by her father's cough. He was alive in a care home thirty miles away. Here, his cough was younger.

sections.title: A different work order
paragraphs: The replacement screw would not take. Leah emptied her tool bag to find a longer one, scattering cable ties and drill bits across the newspaper. Under the children's boots was a sheet of maintenance stationery. Her company's logo was at the top. Her own handwriting filled the description of work.

Return visit required. Do not complete repair. She had signed it with the shortened signature she used when she was tired. The date was tomorrow's. Beneath it, in another ink, someone had written: She always forgets why she left.

Leah turned toward the elevator. Her bag still held the doors apart, but the opening had narrowed. Through it she could see the real fifth-floor landing, its white paint and bicycle rack. A woman stood there holding a phone. Her hair was gray. She was staring straight at Leah, moving her mouth.

Leah leaned close enough to hear. 'Don't fix the handle,' the older woman said. She had Leah's old apprentice scar across her thumb. 'It only opens when you've finished. And once you've finished, there's always another thing that needs you.' Behind her, someone began knocking on a door Leah could not see.

Her mother sighed. 'You were always good at finding reasons to go.' She did not sound angry. That was worse. Leah looked down at the boots. They were her size when she was seven. The newspaper beneath them carried a photograph of a missing technician. In the photograph, she was wearing the jacket she had put on that morning.

sections.title: Unfinished
paragraphs: The loose handle turned. On the other side, her father called her by the nickname no one at work knew. Leah put the longer screw back in its box. Then she removed the screw already in the door, placed it in her pocket, and said, 'I can't finish this today.'

Her mother stood. For a moment the radiator stopped hissing and the whole landing smelled of cold concrete. 'When will you come back?' she asked. Leah had spent years regretting every answer she had given too quickly. This time she took her time. 'I don't know.'

She lifted the tool bag out of the doorway. The older woman beyond the gap reached toward her, then stopped, as though remembering something. Leah stepped into the car. The doors shut on the cardigan, the boots, the small familiar kitchen sounds. On the display, five appeared.

The caretaker found her sitting on the elevator floor. He said she had been inside for ninety seconds. Leah asked for the building's original plans. A service void ran between the fourth and fifth floors, eighteen inches high. Nothing had ever been built there.

She drove to the care home instead of returning to the office. Her father was annoyed that she had missed dinner, then pleased with the sandwich she brought. She stayed while he told a story she had heard many times. When he fell asleep, she sat beside the bed, turning the stripped screw between her fingers.

The next morning her work order had disappeared from the system. In its place was a repeat call for Calder House, entered at 2:14 a.m. The fault description was three words long: Handle still loose. Leah marked the job unsafe, called her supervisor, and kept the screw.

title: The Voice Left on Side B
deck: A sound archivist restores an anonymous cassette. Its missing voice begins borrowing the small sounds from her flat, one recording at a time.

sections.title: Room tone
paragraphs: Ada made her living rescuing voices from damaged tape. She had cleaned wedding speeches, interviews with retired miners, and one entire hour of a man attempting to teach his parrot a telephone number. She knew the difference between silence and a recording of an empty room. The anonymous cassette contained neither.

It arrived in a padded envelope with no return address. A handwritten label read HOUSE RECORDING, SIDE A. Beneath that, in smaller letters: Leave the other side alone. Ada photographed the label, logged the donation, and listened to Side A through her studio headphones.

There was a kettle, a chair moving, somebody opening a window. After nine minutes a woman's voice said, 'That's everything, I think.' The window shut. The tape kept turning, carrying a soft hiss that changed whenever Ada moved her head. It felt oddly like listening to a room through a keyhole.

She turned the cassette over to check whether Side B had been erased. The first sound was her own kettle clicking off. Not a similar kettle. Hers had a loose lid that rattled twice before the switch released. On the tape, it rattled twice. From her kitchen came a bright mechanical click, without its usual rattle.

Ada took off her headphones and put the kettle on again. Steam lifted the lid. It trembled visibly. She heard nothing until the switch clicked. On the recording, the missing rattle played once more, followed by the scrape of a chair.

sections.title: The inventory
paragraphs: She spent half an hour finding explanations. Fatigue. A blocked ear. An electrical fault in the kettle. Then she pulled out her kitchen chair. Its rubber foot caught on the floor in the usual short stutter, but the movement was silent. In the headphones, somebody dragged a chair across a room.

She stopped the deck. The flat settled around her. The refrigerator hummed, traffic passed, a neighbor laughed. She could hear perfectly well. On her desk, the cassette counter stood at 0037. Her digital capture showed thirty-seven seconds of sound, ending with the click of her own mouse.

Ada clicked the mouse. The button moved beneath her finger without making a noise. She played the capture through the computer speakers. Kettle, chair, mouse. After each sound came a short inhalation. Someone was listening back. She had restored hundreds of breaths, softened their harshness, removed them when clients asked. This one seemed to be getting easier.

She searched the archive's accession book for the envelope's postmark. There was an older donation from the same town: household recordings, fifteen cassettes, withdrawn by the donor in 1988. A note clipped to the record said the donor had requested that every copy be destroyed. The archivist had written, No copies made. Underneath, in a different hand: Ask what he means by copies.

Ada called the number on the old form. It had been disconnected. She called her colleague Martin instead and described the problem badly enough that he asked whether she had eaten. She tried to laugh. Her throat moved. Over the phone Martin said, 'Ada? Are you still there?'

sections.title: A voice assembled
paragraphs: She touched her throat. 'Yes,' she said. The word came out normally. Relief made her laugh again, and the laugh made no sound. On the computer, the digital capture had grown longer even though she had stopped recording. At its end, a woman laughed with Ada's small catch between breaths.

The capture was acquiring the flat's sounds in the order they had been taken. After the laugh came footsteps, the zipper of her jacket, a cough. Ada watched the waveform extend. She unplugged the computer. The speakers gave one final soft breath as their power light went dark.

The cassette itself was warm. Against the window she could see the strip of tape inside the shell, a brown ribbon wound around its little white wheels. The label on Side A had lifted at one corner. Under it were words pressed so hard into the paper that they had marked the plastic: It cannot finish a voice you do not use.

Ada understood why the original donor had asked about copies. Her capture had not reproduced the sound. It had made another place for the listener to wait. She thought of cloud backups, automatic uploads, the archive's preservation server. The network cable lay disconnected beside her laptop. She worked from home because the archive could not afford to heat her studio every evening. For once, the economy had helped.

She wrote Martin a message asking him to come, then stopped before sending it. The keyboard had fallen silent beneath her fingers. On the dark computer's speakers, keys began tapping. A voice was practicing her name, using her laugh for the first syllable.

sections.title: The last sound
paragraphs: Ada worked with the headphones off. She erased the local capture, removed the laptop's battery, and pulled the ribbon from the cassette with a pencil. Every few feet, a room sound returned: the mouse click, the zipper, her chair scraping across the floor. The tape came out in tangled loops. In the kitchen, the kettle began rattling though it was cold.

At the very end of the ribbon was a clear leader with no magnetic coating. Knotted around it was a short length of older brown tape. Ada held it up to the desk lamp. The knot had been tied by hand. Someone else had reached this point and decided that a warning was enough.

From the unplugged speakers came her mother's voice. It asked Ada to wait. Ada's mother was alive, away on a walking holiday, and had never been recorded in this flat. The thing had learned what a plea should sound like. Ada cut through the knot and the clear leader together.

The refrigerator stopped. So did the traffic and the neighbor's television. For a few seconds she stood in a silence so complete that she felt her heartbeat in her teeth. Then a truck passed below the window. Her kettle's lid clicked as the metal cooled. Ada laughed once, shakily, and heard herself.

Martin arrived twenty minutes later. He found her sorting the ruined tape into a metal biscuit tin. He asked whether she could play him what she had heard. Ada said no, and he accepted that with less explanation than she expected. They drank coffee in the kitchen. She could hear his spoon against the china. He left his phone switched off on the table.

She did not send the tin anywhere. She kept it in the archive's locked cupboard, with an honest description and no listening copy. Sometimes a new colleague asked why its catalog entry had no audio sample. Ada always answered in person, away from microphones, and made sure they heard every word.

title: The Window That Stayed Lit
deck: Working nights, a translator begins exchanging notes with a neighbor across the courtyard. Then the neighbor asks why his room has no door.

sections.title: Another night worker
paragraphs: For the first month in the flat, Daniel's only neighbor was a square of yellow light across the courtyard. Other windows darkened after midnight. That one stayed lit until dawn. Behind it an older woman sat at a table, her hands moving over something too small for Daniel to see.

He translated technical manuals at night because his clients were eight time zones away. The courtyard was narrow enough to hear a teaspoon dropped in another kitchen, yet neither of them made much noise. Sometimes the woman looked up when he did. Eventually they began raising their cups to each other.

One Thursday she held a sheet of paper against the glass. TEA OR COFFEE? Daniel wrote COFFEE on the back of a printer invoice. She shook her head and held up a second page: THAT EXPLAINS THE HOURS. He laughed louder than he had meant to. It startled him to realize she could probably hear it.

Her name was Ruth. She repaired old books for a charity shop, working through the night when her hands would not let her sleep. Daniel told her about a manual that contained eleven different names for the same valve. Ruth wrote: SOME THINGS NEED MORE THAN ONE NAME. Then, beneath it: MY SON CALLS ME ON SUNDAYS.

By the following week their windows had become a small appointment. Daniel began keeping a spare pad on the sill. He bought better coffee. When Ruth missed a night, he stayed at his desk until six, worrying that he had mistaken a brief acquaintance for something he was entitled to keep.

sections.title: The question on the glass
paragraphs: She returned the next evening with a new book and an apology written across two sheets. Daniel asked whether she was all right. Ruth nodded, then frowned past him. She pointed at the wall behind his chair. He turned to look at his bookshelf, the narrow hallway, his kitchen door.

When he turned back, she was holding a question: WHERE IS YOUR DOOR? Daniel circled his finger toward the hallway. Ruth looked more troubled. She drew a rectangle containing a table and a chair, surrounded on all four sides by a wall. A little figure sat at the table. Above it she had written his name.

He stood and walked into the hallway. From the kitchen he heard three sharp knocks. Ruth was tapping her window with her knuckles. When Daniel returned, she was waving both hands for him to stop. The next page said: YOU DID NOT GET UP.

Daniel looked behind his chair. A second chair stood between him and the hall, identical to the one he had left. On it lay his jacket, arranged as though someone had just slipped out of it. He touched the collar. It was warm. His own chair, the one by the window, now had the jacket too.

He called his landlord. The phone rang inside the wall beside the bookshelf. Daniel knew that particular ringtone; the landlord used an old song with a trumpet introduction. When he ended the call, the music stopped. Across the courtyard Ruth pressed her whole palm against the glass. DO NOT SIT DOWN, her next page said.

sections.title: Someone at the table
paragraphs: He tried the hallway again. This time it ended after two steps in a wall painted the same gray as his bedroom. He knocked, hard enough to hurt. A patient knock answered from the other side, one beat after his own. The apartment smelled of fresh paint and warm printer paper.

At the window Ruth held up a larger drawing. It showed the courtyard, her room, and Daniel's room opposite. Every other window was crossed out. Beside Daniel she had drawn a seated figure in heavy pencil. She pointed to his chair, then covered her eyes.

He understood enough to stop looking at the desk. Whatever sat there was becoming easier to see. A hand rested on the invoice beneath his first message. Its fingers had the old yellow nicotine stains Daniel's father had carried, though Daniel had never smoked. He stared at Ruth's window instead. 'What do I do?' he shouted.

She cupped a hand to her ear. The courtyard took his words and returned them in a dry flutter, like pages turning. Ruth wrote: TELL ME SOMETHING I DO NOT KNOW. Daniel shouted his full name. She shook her head and pointed behind him. From the chair, someone recited it in Daniel's voice.

He thought of work, his school, the addresses where he had lived. All were written somewhere, filed in envelopes or stored in a machine. Then he remembered his sister learning to swim. For three summers she had refused to enter a pool unless he called the water soup. He had not thought about it in years.

'My sister thought the swimming pool was soup,' he shouted. The voice behind him stumbled over the word. Ruth leaned forward. Daniel told her about his sister's orange armbands, their father's terrible sandwiches, the cold tile where they waited for her courage. By the time he reached the sandwiches, Ruth was laughing.

sections.title: A place to knock
paragraphs: In the hallway, something clicked. Daniel kept talking. He told Ruth about the first sentence he had ever been paid to translate, and the shame of buying flowers for himself and claiming they were a gift. Behind him, the other voice grew quieter. It could repeat his facts. It could not quite tell his stories before he did.

Ruth disappeared from her window. Daniel almost turned toward the chair. Then he heard running footsteps above the courtyard, followed by a door slamming and a knock in his hallway. Three knocks. He walked toward them without looking back. The wall at the end of the hall now held his front door.

He opened it on a woman in slippers, carrying a pad thick with taped-together pages. She was much shorter than he had imagined. 'You really do need better coffee,' she said. Daniel stepped outside. Behind him, his apartment light went out. They stood together while someone on the other side carefully turned the key.

The landlord found nothing wrong the next morning. One chair, one jacket, a perfectly ordinary hallway. Daniel moved his desk into the living room, where visitors could see it from the door. He stopped working through every night. Ruth gave him a book she had repaired, its spine stronger than the original.

They still live across the courtyard. On Sundays Daniel sometimes carries her groceries upstairs. They do not leave notes at the windows anymore. Once, while Ruth was away visiting her son, the yellow square lit up at three in the morning. A sheet of white paper appeared against the glass. Daniel closed his curtains before it could turn around.

title: The Parcel for Apartment Zero
deck: A courier accepts one final delivery to an apartment that does not exist. Inside the parcel is a way out, provided he can keep it unopened.

sections.title: The extra stop
paragraphs: Owen's last delivery was not on the route when he loaded the van. It appeared after he finished his final scheduled stop: 18 Bell Lane, Apartment 0. One small parcel, no recipient name, signature required. The dispatch office had closed ten minutes earlier. The app offered him a late-delivery bonus large enough to cover the petrol.

He found the parcel beneath his empty crate. It was wrapped in plain brown paper, unusually careful at the corners, and weighed about as much as a book. Someone had written DO NOT OPEN IN THE BUILDING along the seam. Owen had seen stranger instructions. He photographed the label and drove to Bell Lane.

Number eighteen had six brass bells. They began at one. He rang the caretaker, who told him there was no apartment zero and that couriers always confused this building with the one around the corner. Owen checked the pin on the map. It pulsed directly beneath his feet.

While he was explaining, the intercom crackled. A second voice said, 'I'll take that.' The latch released. Through the glass door, Owen saw a narrow staircase leading down beside the main stairs. A light burned at its foot. He could have sworn the staircase had been a cupboard a moment earlier.

At the bottom was a gray door with a round brass plate. On it, freshly polished, was a zero. Owen knocked. Somewhere behind the door, a chair moved. Then a voice he had not heard for six years said, 'Leave it outside, mate. I'll get it in a minute.'

sections.title: A familiar excuse
paragraphs: His brother used to say that through his bedroom door when he wanted to be left alone. Adam was not dead. He had moved abroad after a family argument and stopped answering calls. Owen had spent years composing messages that sounded casual enough to send. He never sent most of them.

'Adam?' The light at the top of the stairs went out. Owen looked back and found himself facing a second gray door, identical to the first. Where the main entrance should have been was another brass zero. His phone showed no signal. On the delivery screen, the recipient field had filled itself in: OWEN REED.

Behind the first door, his brother laughed. 'You took your time.' Owen moved the parcel away from the threshold. Something inside tapped once against the paper. He thought of a book sliding in its box, then felt a second tap directly beneath his thumb. The sound was too deliberate.

A woman spoke through the second door. 'Please don't answer him.' Owen turned. A piece of card slid under it. Printed on one side was an old delivery company's logo. On the other, in small neat writing: The parcel belongs outside. You are carrying the address in with you.

She said her name was Irene. She had delivered flowers here, years ago, to someone whose funeral she had attended. 'I opened the wrapping to see who sent them,' she said. 'You mustn't.' Owen asked how to get out. Irene went quiet long enough that he could hear her breathing through the keyhole. 'Find the place where you first knocked.'

sections.title: The wrong doors
paragraphs: The corridor had acquired a turn. Owen followed it past four gray doors, each marked zero. Behind one, a television played the theme from a program his father used to watch. Behind another, someone was frying onions. The air was thick with the comforting smells of other people's dinners.

He took a photograph to mark the turn. In the picture, the corridor stretched straight ahead. There were no doors, only a concrete wall and the shadow of a staircase. A dark shape stood behind his shoulder. Owen lowered the phone and did not look around. The parcel grew heavier in his hands.

He found a fire-exit sign with an arrow pointing into the wall. Beneath it was a faded rectangle where another sign had been removed. A courier's initials were scratched into the paint: I.M. He knocked on the nearest door and asked whether Irene was still there. No answer. On the floor he found a dry black rose tied with delivery ribbon.

The first door had a scratch below its handle. Owen remembered making it with the corner of his scanner when he knocked. He went back, searching every handle. The voice behind each door became more insistent. His brother offered him a drink. His father asked him to stop making a fuss. Someone who sounded exactly like Owen begged him to put down the box.

At last he found the scratch. It was below a handle on a door that had no number. Owen touched the cut in the paint. Through the parcel came a rush of street sounds: a bus braking, rainwater in a gutter, someone wheeling a bin over paving stones. He held the package to his ear. The street was very close.

He nearly tore open the seam. Instead he remembered Irene's flowers. He put the parcel against the unnumbered door and listened. The street sounds moved through the wood. On the paper, his printed name faded. Beyond the door, Adam said, 'You can't leave me here again.'

sections.title: Outside
paragraphs: Owen had no practiced answer to that. For six years he had imagined Adam admitting fault first. He stood on a nonexistent landing and finally said the less satisfying thing. 'I should have called you.' From the other side came a long, irritated sigh. It sounded like a person running out of lines to read.

He kept one hand flat against the parcel and turned the handle with the other. The door opened on Bell Lane. His van stood across the road with its hazard lights blinking. Owen pushed the parcel over the threshold before he stepped through. Inside the wrapping, something knocked so hard that a corner split.

He left it on the pavement and went back to hold the door open. 'Irene,' he called. A woman in an old blue delivery coat emerged from the dark. She had one shoe and a string of identification cards around her neck. Owen took her arm. As she crossed the threshold, the wrapping collapsed around a handful of dead flowers.

The caretaker found them beside a cupboard containing mops and a broken stepladder. Irene gave the police her name, her old address, and the name of her employer. She kept asking whether it was still October. Owen stayed with her until someone brought a blanket. His delivery app listed the final stop as canceled.

The bonus never arrived. Owen paid for his own petrol. Then he called the number he still had for Adam and left a message without rehearsing it. Three days later, while he was loading the van, his phone rang. His brother sounded older. The conversation was awkward, ordinary, and considerably harder than opening a door. Owen stayed on the line.

title: The Room That Kept the Rain
deck: During a summer drought, a hotel cleaner finds rain falling inside an unused room. The water is rising toward the ceiling, and something is waiting above it.

sections.title: The dry season
paragraphs: By the thirty-eighth day without rain, the hotel had stopped watering its window boxes. Nadia carried drinking water to work because the taps ran brown each morning. At seven, while she was folding sheets on the second-floor landing, she heard a downpour behind the door of Room 209.

The room had been out of use since she joined the hotel. Its lock took an old metal key instead of a card. The owner said the bathroom needed work and that she should leave it alone. Now a thin line of water showed beneath the door, darkening the carpet without spreading any farther.

Nadia knocked. No answer. She fetched a bucket, used the key, and pushed the door inward. Rain fell through the room in fine silver threads. It came from the carpet and rose toward the ceiling. The bed stood beneath it, its blankets lifting and settling as though someone had just climbed out.

She stayed at the threshold. The air smelled of wet leaves, quite different from the hot tarmac outside. A drop struck the underside of her chin. It traveled upward over her cheek and vanished into her hair. On the ceiling, water gathered in a dark, rippling pool.

Nadia closed the door and called the owner. He let her explain without interrupting. Then he asked whether she had moved anything. When she said no, he told her to lock the room and wait in reception. He was not coming to the hotel. He was leaving town.

sections.title: The old photograph
paragraphs: Nadia did not wait in reception. Seven guests were eating breakfast, and one had already complained that the ceiling above his shower felt damp. She asked the porter, Luis, to help her inspect the top floor. He was older than the owner and had a habit of carrying keys to doors that no longer existed.

At the mention of 209 he put down his coffee. He showed her a photograph in the back office: the hotel beside a river, a low iron bridge visible through the ground-floor windows. Nadia knew the river. It ran behind the hotel, deep in a concrete channel. The bridge in the photograph had been removed long before she was born.

A storm had flooded the ground floor in 1963, Luis said. The owner at the time had paid to have every damaged room stripped and replastered. Except one. In 209, above the flood line, a guest had woken to find river water across the ceiling. Her traveling case was still there when they opened the room. She was not.

'It happens when the river gets low,' Luis said. He had seen it twice before. Both times the former owner had waited for rain, and both times the room had dried by morning. The present owner had sold the old contents online in April. Nadia looked at the photograph again. A brass disk hung beside the reception bell. She had seen its pale outline on the wall.

Luis opened the old inventory. The missing disk was a flood marker salvaged from the bridge. Its description included a warning scratched into its reverse: KEEP ABOVE WATER. In the auction photograph, the buyer had displayed it face down beside a ruler. Behind its reflected edge, Nadia could make out part of a wet hand.

sections.title: The high-water mark
paragraphs: By ten, water had reached the ceiling outside 209. It hung in a long shallow ribbon above the hallway, reflecting the carpet beneath it. Nadia looked up and saw a lamp swinging below an iron bridge. The view had depth. Somewhere beyond the plaster, a current was passing in the dark.

She asked the guests to leave and called the fire service. The man on the phone asked where the water was entering. Nadia tried to explain. While she spoke, a suitcase rose slowly from the carpet, turned on its handle, and slid into the ceiling without leaving a hole. She stopped explaining and said the building was unsafe.

Luis had found the buyer's address. A dealer fifteen minutes away had put the marker in his shop window. Nadia drove there in her work clothes. The dealer was standing on the pavement, staring at the glass. Behind it, old clocks and porcelain plates hung at different heights in a room filling from the top down.

She broke a small corner of the shop window with the tire iron from her car. Water spilled inward through the gap, against the heat of the pavement. The marker lay on the sill, its brass face perfectly dry. Nadia hooked it with the tire iron and pulled it outside. Every object in the shop fell at once.

On the back, beneath the scratched warning, the brass had been rubbed smooth by many hands. Nadia wrapped it in a towel. The towel grew heavy and cold. From inside it came the slow clanking sound of chains beneath a bridge. She drove with both windows open and kept her eyes on the road.

sections.title: Above the water
paragraphs: Luis was waiting outside the hotel. The emergency crew had cleared the building and were checking the river wall. Nadia showed a firefighter the old photograph and the disk. He was looking at it when a chair passed the second-floor window, drifting upward with all four legs pointing toward the sky.

Nadia and Luis went in with two firefighters. The old hook beside the reception bell was still dry, but water trembled along the ceiling, lower than before. Through its surface Nadia saw ironwork and a pale, upturned face. The face moved with them as they crossed the lobby. It was not a reflection.

She could not lift the disk without standing on a chair. Luis held it steady while the firefighter passed her the towel. As she raised her arms, the cold surface above her bent downward. Fingers pressed against it from the other side. They spread carefully, testing where her head would be.

Nadia found the hook by touch. The disk's loop slipped off once. Water closed over the crown of her head, and for a moment she heard a river hammering against stone. She pushed upward again. The loop caught. Luis pulled her down so hard that the chair overturned beneath her.

The water withdrew without falling. It streamed up the walls toward 209, carrying the sound of loose chains. In the sudden quiet, they heard a single suitcase wheel rolling across the floor above them. The firefighter helped Nadia outside. Her hair was dry. One of her earrings was gone.

The hotel never reopened. The disk remains high on the reception wall, checked each month by someone from the town. Nadia works in a supermarket now. When rain finally came that summer, she stood beneath the loading-bay roof and watched it fall in the proper direction. In the gutter at her feet, something small and silver turned once. She let the water carry it away.

title: The Last Passenger on the Night Line
deck: On her final shift, a train conductor finds a passenger holding a ticket for a station closed forty years ago. He has been trying to get off for a very long time.

sections.title: One more ticket
paragraphs: Mira had a retirement card in her bag and nine minutes left on the last train when she found the man in the rear carriage. He wore a dark suit with a paper flower in its buttonhole. Beside him sat a small cake box, held level on a folded coat. He offered his ticket before she asked.

It was a stiff rectangle of yellow card, the kind Mira had used as a child. A neat round hole had been punched through the fare. The destination was Vale End. She read it twice. Vale End had closed forty years earlier, when a landslide destroyed the little station and the line was diverted through the hill.

'I'm afraid we don't stop there,' she said. The man nodded as though she had told him something about the weather. 'I know. I keep hoping they'll put it back.' He looked at the cake box. 'It's getting rather late.'

Mira asked where he actually needed to go. He gave an address in a village the new route no longer served. She could arrange a taxi from the terminus, she said. The man thanked her, but when the train entered the tunnel his face became difficult to see. The paper flower remained clear against his lapel.

She looked toward the connecting door. There were three more passengers in the next carriage. They sat very straight, each holding an old yellow ticket. Mira had checked that carriage at the previous stop. It had been empty.

sections.title: The old route
paragraphs: She called the driver on the internal radio. Rafi said the instruments were normal, but the tunnel was taking longer than it should. Mira told him about the tickets. He did not laugh. Instead, he asked whether the passengers had bags. She looked through the connecting door. A shopping basket, a child's satchel, a violin case. 'Yes,' she said. Rafi swore softly.

His first instructor had told him a story about the old line. During the last evening service before the landslide, a signal failure had stopped the train short of Vale End. The passengers walked back along the track toward the station. There had been heavy rain. Some never reached it. Their belongings were recovered in the cutting.

Mira remembered the incident. Her father had worked on the recovery team, and for weeks afterward he had come home carrying his boots in a plastic bag. He never told her what he had found. Rafi said they should keep moving. As long as the train stayed on the new line, the tunnel had to end.

The man in the suit was listening. 'It does end,' he said. 'That's the trouble.' He opened the cake box. Inside was a small cake with white icing, its careful lettering blurred by condensation: WELCOME HOME, JUNE. A narrow slice had been cut from it. The cut surface was fresh.

'My wife came home from the hospital that afternoon,' he said. 'Nothing dramatic. A new hip. I thought she'd be tired of their puddings.' He smiled, embarrassed by his own explanation. Then the train lights dimmed. Across the aisle, the dark window showed a platform with a wooden bench and a white-painted sign: VALE END.

sections.title: The announcement
paragraphs: Mira put her hand against the window. They were still moving. She could feel the wheels beneath her feet. But the platform stayed level with the carriage, its bench and station sign holding perfectly still. Beyond it, people waited beneath umbrellas. None looked toward the train.

The man stood. So did the passengers in the next carriage. Along the train, connecting doors opened in succession. Mira saw more yellow tickets, more faces reflected in glass. The radio hissed. Rafi said the controls were not responding. The speedometer still read fifty, but the platform had appeared outside his cab too.

The man in the suit pressed the door button. Nothing happened. He pressed again. His hand began to shake. 'Every time,' he said. The woman with the shopping basket reached past him, then withdrew her hand. From the other carriages came a quiet, patient sound of people trying handles.

Mira looked at her watch. The second hand was moving backward. In the window beside her face was the reflection of a girl in a school uniform, clutching a lunchbox. Mira had carried that lunchbox the year her father stopped working on the railway. She took her hand away from the glass. The girl did not.

She asked the man whether anyone had ever told them they had arrived. He looked puzzled. In forty years, perhaps everyone had done what she first did: explained that the station was closed. A conductor knew the difference between a place existing and a journey being allowed to end. Mira reached for the public-address handset.

'We are now arriving at Vale End,' she said. Her voice sounded small in the long train. 'This service terminates here. Please take all your belongings with you.' The man closed his cake box. The platform lamps came on, one after another.

sections.title: End of service
paragraphs: The doors opened. Cold air moved through the carriage, carrying wet earth and the sharp smell of creosote. The passengers stepped down without hurrying. Mira counted them because counting was something she could still do. Twenty-three. The last was the man with the cake. He turned and offered her the small paper flower.

She almost took it. Then she saw that the girl in the window had moved into the aisle. She stood exactly where Mira stood, reaching for the flower with a much smaller hand. On the platform, beneath one of the umbrellas, Mira recognized her father. He looked as he had before his illness. He had been dead for nine years.

Rafi spoke in her ear, very clearly. 'Mira. Stay with the train.' She lowered her hand. The girl took one step toward the open door and vanished. On the platform, her father nodded once, as though she had answered a question correctly. Mira told the man with the cake to keep his flower.

She checked the carriage one last time. The seats were empty. The old yellow ticket lay on the floor, its round hole dark against the vinyl. She picked it up and held it through the doorway. The man took it with two fingers. Then Mira pressed the close button and waited until every light above the doors had gone out.

The tunnel ended. Rafi brought the train into the terminus three minutes late. No one on the platform noticed anything unusual about the empty carriages or the two railway workers standing together beside the cab. Mira called home before collecting her retirement cake from the staff room.

In the morning she found something in her bag beneath the card. It was her old lunchbox, clean and empty. On its lid, her father had written her name in the black marker he used for his tools. Mira washed it, dried it carefully, and began taking it on walks. When someone asked where she was going, she found she enjoyed being able to choose.

title: Three Stories for a Sleepless Night
deck: A sound behind a wall, a reflection that lingers, and a voice from beneath the bed. Three original tales of things that should not answer back.

sections.title: The room on the other side
paragraphs: The scratching began after the last bus passed the house. Mara knew the sound of mice. Mice hurried and stopped. This moved slowly, from the bedroom door to the window, as though someone were dragging a single fingernail along the other side of the plaster.

At breakfast, she knocked on the wall to show the landlord where it had happened. Three knocks. He looked at the wardrobe, then at the ceiling, and told her the building had no room on that side. Beyond the wall was open air.

That night she moved her bed across the room. The scratching followed. At two in the morning it stopped behind her pillow, although the pillow was now against the opposite wall. She held her breath. From inside the plaster, someone held theirs.

Mara found a photograph in the hallway the next morning: the house before the extension, a garden where her bedroom stood, and a woman looking through a window that no longer existed. On the back, in fresh pencil, were three words: Stop knocking back.

sections.title: The last person in the mirror
paragraphs: Eli always covered the hallway mirror before a storm. It was one of his grandmother's habits, and he had kept it for the same reason he kept her teacups: some things were easier to preserve than explain.
One evening the cloth slipped. Lightning showed him his own reflection halfway up the stairs. Eli was standing at the bottom. In the dark between flashes he heard a shoe touch the next step.

He reached for the cloth, but his reflection put a finger to its lips. There was someone behind it in the glass, a tall shape folded to fit beneath the ceiling. The reflection was not warning Eli to be quiet. It was asking him to listen.

Eli covered the mirror and spent the night in the kitchen. In the morning the stairs were dry and empty, except for two wet footprints on the inside of the glass. One faced up the stairs. The other faced out.

sections.title: The question under the bed
paragraphs: Nora dropped her phone beneath the bed and called it from the kitchen. In the bedroom, the ringtone stopped after one note. Then her own recorded voice said, very softly, 'I'm here.'

She checked the screen on the kitchen phone. The call was still connecting. She ended it. The voice in the bedroom kept talking, listing ordinary things: the coat on the chair, the book on the floor, the hand resting beside the mattress.

Nora had left the bedroom door open. From the hall she could see the coat and the book. She could not see a hand. She stepped backwards until her shoulders touched the front door, keeping the gap beneath the bed in sight.

Her missing phone slid into the hallway. Its screen displayed an incoming call from her number. Nora did not answer. A moment later, the voice beneath the bed asked a new question: 'If you're out there, who is lying up here?'

sections.title: Keep the light on for one more page
paragraphs: These tales use ordinary spaces as their starting point. The fear comes from one small detail refusing to behave as expected. For more fictional encounters, explore the related videos and stories below.

title: Five Camera-Inspired Horror Stories
deck: A familiar room can become a different place when you watch the recording. Five fictional scenes about cameras that seem to know more than their owners.

sections.title: The visitor between frames
paragraphs: The doorbell camera saved an image every time someone approached the porch. For seven nights, each image showed the same empty chair. On the eighth, the chair was turned towards the house.
Jon put a coin on the seat and watched the live feed. Nothing moved. In the saved photograph, a pale hand was holding the coin. The notification arrived a second later: Familiar face detected.

sections.title: The floor that was not there
paragraphs: An elevator repair technician reviewed a recording after a complaint about an unexpected stop. The camera showed a passenger pressing five, then stepping into a corridor on floor six. The building had only five floors.

The passenger returned before the doors closed. She was older than she had been a moment before. She turned towards the camera and shook her head, once. The technician deleted the recording. The next morning, the button for six had appeared.

sections.title: The other window
paragraphs: A couple left a camera pointing at their living-room window while they travelled. Every afternoon it showed the neighbour watering plants. Every night it showed the reflection of their empty sofa.

On the final evening, the reflected sofa held two people. The couple watched themselves sit perfectly still in their own house. Behind the real sofa, the camera's small red light began to blink. In the hotel, the television switched on.

sections.title: One step behind
paragraphs: The trail camera was supposed to photograph foxes. Instead it collected pictures of a lone hiker, always at the same bend in the path, always carrying a yellow backpack. The dates were different. The pose was identical.
The ranger went to retrieve it. When he opened the case, the camera took one last picture. On the screen, the hiker stood behind him, without the backpack. The ranger was wearing it.

sections.title: The room after midnight
paragraphs: A motion alert woke Asha at 12:03. Her camera showed her bedroom exactly as it was: lamp off, curtains closed, a glass beside the bed. Only the bed was empty.

She was lying in it. She waved a hand in front of the lens. On the recording, the curtains opened instead. Something outside leaned towards the window. Asha reached for the lamp, and a hand in the dark found the switch first.

sections.title: When the screen becomes the storyteller
paragraphs: A camera seems reliable because it records what we miss. In horror fiction, that promise can turn against the viewer: the image becomes the uncertain witness, and the familiar room becomes the mystery. These scenes are invented, not evidence of paranormal events. Watch the related Dark Echo videos for more stories built around unexpected recordings.

title: Ten Fictional Encounters After Dark
deck: A countdown of imagined horror scenes, from an empty lift to a mirror that refuses to follow. Read slowly; the last detail changes each scene.

sections.title: The elevator shadow
paragraphs: A woman stepped into an empty lift. The camera showed a shadow enter with her, though the doors had already closed. At her floor, she stepped out. The shadow stayed behind and pressed the button for her apartment.

sections.title: The hospital curtain
paragraphs: The abandoned ward had been stripped of its beds. One privacy curtain still hung from its rail. When the explorers pulled it aside, they found only a patch of warm floor. Behind them, an invisible monitor began to count a heartbeat.

sections.title: The forest reply
paragraphs: Lost in the trees, Tom called his brother's name. A voice answered from the left. He called again. This time it came from the right, closer. Then his brother's phone rang in his pocket. The message said: Don't follow my voice.

sections.title: The doll on the shelf
paragraphs: The doll faced the wall each morning. June turned it towards the room before bed, convinced the shelf was uneven. One night she stayed awake to watch. The doll did not move. Every other object in the room slowly turned to face it.

sections.title: The spare key
paragraphs: The locked door opened at three. A man stood in the hall holding a key, wearing the coat Ben had buried his father in. Ben could not see his face. The man hung the key on its hook and whispered, 'Someone else has the spare.'

sections.title: The delayed reflection
paragraphs: She raised her hand. The reflection waited. She lowered it. The reflection raised its own hand and pressed one finger against the glass. A tiny crack appeared on her side, and cold air began to move into the room.

sections.title: The final stair
paragraphs: There were twelve stairs to the bedroom. Simon counted thirteen in the dark. At the top he found a door he did not recognise. His mother's voice came from behind it, asking him to come down for breakfast. It had been midnight when he started climbing.

sections.title: The empty shoes
paragraphs: Footsteps crossed the hallway each night. The landlord blamed the pipes until the tenant left a pair of shoes outside the door. In the morning they were worn through at the soles. Inside each one was a folded note: A little further tomorrow.

sections.title: The baby monitor
paragraphs: The baby was asleep beside her when the monitor crackled. From the empty nursery came a soothing voice, humming the song she always sang. Then her own voice said, 'Don't wake him.' Her baby opened his eyes and looked towards the speaker.

sections.title: The face at the lens
paragraphs: The night camera recorded a face inches from its lens. No body entered the frame. The owner turned the camera towards the wall, thinking it was a reflection. The next recording showed the back of the same head. It was looking into the room.

sections.title: One ordinary detail, one impossible change
paragraphs: These are fictional scenes written for entertainment, not a list of verified recordings. Their shared device is a small violation of expectation: an extra stair, a delayed movement, a familiar voice from the wrong place. The related videos below explore the same kind of unsettling storytelling.
